name: Spinach and similar leaves
anchor: Per-produce-class sovereign maximum levels for lead and cadmium (EU Reg. 2023/915 and Switzerland VHK 817.022.15; Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2; AU-NZ Schedule 19; MERCOSUR GMC Res. 12/2011 and Paraguay Decreto 1335/2019; Israel MOH FCS-2016), nickel under EU Reg. 2024/1987, total and inorganic arsenic under MERCOSUR and Israel MOH FCS-2016, and total mercury under Hong Kong Cap. 132V and Israel MOH FCS-2016.
native_basis_label: fresh or frozen spinach as sold, wet weight, edible portion after washing and separation of the edible part
scope_note: Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) and the similar-leaf species that sovereign schedules group with it, plus mustard seedlings, in fresh, baby-leaf and frozen form. This row exists because the sovereign rules split it: EU Reg. 2023/915 writes spinach out of the general leaf-vegetable cadmium row (100 ug/kg) into its own row at 200 ug/kg, Switzerland mirrors that split exactly (Blattgemüse 100 excluding Spinat; Spinat und verwandte Arten 200), and Hong Kong, Thailand, India, Vietnam and Panama all write 'other than spinach' into their leafy-vegetable lead rows. Frozen spinach shares the fresh wet-weight basis; spinach puree, creamed spinach and other prepared forms route to Category 35, and dried spinach powder routes to Category 34. Products marketed for ages 0 to 5 route to Category 1. THE CADMIUM CELL IS THE ONE A HOSTILE EXPERT WILL READ FIRST, so it is argued in full in that cell's substantiation.
basis_guard: wet weight|portion ordinarily consumed|as listed|product as offered to consumer|product as placed on market|as sold|as_sold|as consumed|commodity|edible part
basis_guard_note: Every named anchor for this row must sit in a dietary as-sold, wet-weight, edible-part or portion-ordinarily-consumed basis. The guard rejects the register's article and material bases (toy and food-contact migration, textile and leather extraction, fertiliser and growing-media dry matter, colour-additive ingredient specifications, animal-feed 12 percent moisture), any one of which would be a basis conflation if it anchored a food row.
method: HMTc Method v2.0 (government-limit-only; the strictest applicable sovereign maximum level for the row's product form in the row's native basis, a disclosed read-across where the exact cell is unregulated, a substantiated not-material determination, or a control; never occurrence-derived)

Pb.basis: wet weight, fresh spinach as sold
Pb.label: AU-NZ Food Standards Code Schedule 19 sets lead at 100 ug/kg for vegetables except brassicas, which covers spinach as a matter of Australian and New Zealand law; the EU leaf-vegetable row (whose scope note records that it covers spinach), its Swiss mirror, MERCOSUR, Paraguay and Israel all sit at 300 ug/kg.
Pb.substantiation: Spinach is not a brassica, so the AU-NZ 100 ug/kg row applies to it directly with no interpretation. It is the strictest applicable sovereign lead maximum level for this exact product form and is selected on that basis. Hong Kong's leafy-vegetable lead row is expressly 'other than spinach' and is therefore not applicable to this row and is not named.

Cd.basis: wet weight, fresh spinach as sold
Cd.label: AU-NZ Food Standards Code Schedule 19 sets cadmium at 100 ug/kg for leafy vegetables with no spinach carve-out, which caps spinach in Australia and New Zealand; the EU spinach row, its Swiss mirror, Hong Kong, MERCOSUR, Paraguay and Israel all sit at 200 ug/kg.
Cd.substantiation: This is the cell where the instruments genuinely disagree, so the reasoning is stated in full. The EU wrote spinach out of the 100 ug/kg leaf-vegetable row into a 200 ug/kg row precisely because spinach accumulates more cadmium than other leaves, and Switzerland, Hong Kong, MERCOSUR and Israel are at 200 ug/kg as well. AU-NZ Schedule 19 has no spinach carve-out: its cadmium entry is 'leafy vegetables 0.1 mg/kg', which caps spinach sold in Australia and New Zealand at 100 ug/kg. HMTc binds 100 ug/kg. Achievability is deliberately not an input to this selection, because feasibility-selected numeric rationales are retired under Method v2.0; the only question the method asks is which applicable sovereign maximum level is strictest, and a published value of 200 ug/kg would certify spinach lots that are unlawful in two of the twelve credible jurisdictions. The gap between the EU and AU-NZ treatments is stated, not hidden, and no occurrence evidence was consulted in choosing between them.

tAs.basis: wet weight, fresh spinach as sold
tAs.label: MERCOSUR GMC Res. 12/2011 and Paraguay Decreto 1335/2019 set total arsenic for leaf vegetables including loose-leaf brassicas and fresh aromatic herbs at 300 ug/kg; Hong Kong sets 500 ug/kg for vegetables and Israel 1000 ug/kg.
tAs.substantiation: No jurisdiction writes a spinach-specific total-arsenic maximum level, so the general leaf-vegetable rows of each instrument are the applicable cells for this product form. The inorganic-arsenic species limit of 60 ug/kg is the operative arsenic constraint.

iAs.rationale: No in-force sovereign or general-food iAs maximum level applies to this product on the dietary-content basis after the supersession of regulations/israel-moh-fcs-2016-heavy-metals-tin-food-guidelines; the species is bounded by its parent total (tAs) per the certification-readiness ruling (species ≤ total).

tHg.basis: wet weight, fresh spinach as sold
tHg.label: Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 12 sets total mercury for vegetables other than edible fungi at 10 ug/kg; Israel MOH FCS-2016 category 3 sets 30 ug/kg for fruits and vegetables.
tHg.substantiation: Hong Kong's vegetable row has no spinach carve-out for mercury and is the strictest applicable sovereign total-mercury maximum level for this product form. Edible fungi are expressly outside it and route to Category 29.

MeHg.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets a methylmercury maximum level for this product form, and no not-material determination is supportable for it: the routed corpus quantifies methylmercury in edible plant and fungal tissue (wang2021-houttuynia-mercury-china measured methylmercury in the leaf and root tissue of an edible leafy vegetable at an LOD of 0.002 ug/kg; stasinos2014-heavy-metals-tubers-review in root and tuber tissue; asensio2023-madrid-mushrooms-mercury), so the species is not absent from produce and the biological premise of a not-material determination is rebutted inside this very category. Spinach is a leaf vegetable, so wang2021-houttuynia-mercury-china is a measurement in the same tissue type and the same product class as this row; the sibling leafy-vegetables-other, non-root-vegetables and root-tuber-vegetables rows reject the same not-material claim on the same evidence, and this row is aligned with them rather than published on the opposite treatment. Methylmercury is therefore held under mandatory analytical control rather than recorded not-material, and it remains bounded by identity below the published total-mercury ceiling for this row (Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 12, 10 ug/kg); methylmercury cannot exceed total mercury. No methylmercury ceiling is invented.
MeHg.reference_method: Methylmercury by GC-ICP-MS or EN 16801, required only on a lot whose total mercury reaches 60 percent of the published total-mercury ceiling; any quantifiable methylmercury on such a lot is investigated and the lot is held pending root-cause analysis.

Ni.basis: wet weight, fresh spinach as sold
Ni.label: EU Reg. 2024/1987 sets nickel for leafy vegetables except fresh herbs at 500 ug/kg, mirrored by Switzerland VHK Blattgemüse.
Ni.substantiation: Spinach is a leafy vegetable and not a fresh herb, so the EU leafy-vegetable nickel row applies directly. No jurisdiction writes a spinach-specific nickel maximum level.

Sn.rationale: Every tin maximum level in the register is scoped to canned product: EU Reg. 2023/915 sets 200000 ug/kg for canned foods and 100000 ug/kg for canned beverages, Codex CXS 193-1995 and AU-NZ Schedule 19 set 250000 ug/kg for canned foods, and Hong Kong Cap. 132V sets 250000 ug/kg for canned food other than canned beverages. Those limits regulate one contamination pathway, dissolution of tin from tinplate into the packed food. This row is not packed in tinplate, so the pathway that every sovereign tin limit addresses is physically absent and any tin present is dietary background rather than packaging migration. Fresh and frozen spinach is sold loose, bagged or in polymer clamshells. Hermetically sealed tinplate presentations of this commodity route to the canned-foods row in Category 7 and carry the canned-foods tin maximum level there.
Sn.reference_method: Total tin by ICP-MS on every lot as part of the mandatory eight-totals panel; a result above 50 ug/kg is investigated for a metal-contact source in harvest, wash, transport or packing before the lot is released.
Sn.regulatory_basis: No jurisdiction sets a tin maximum level for non-canned produce; all tin maximum levels in the register are conditioned on a canned (tinplate) presentation, and the EU rows expressly exclude canned dried and canned powdered products from even that scope.
Sn.jurisdictions_checked: EU Reg. 2023/915; EU Reg. 2024/1987 (nickel); Switzerland VHK 817.022.15 (2026 metal/metalloid annex); Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2 Schedule; AU-NZ Food Standards Code Schedule 19; MERCOSUR GMC Res. 12/2011 and Paraguay Decreto 1335/2019; Israel MOH FCS-2016; Codex CXS 193-1995; US FDA (21 CFR, action levels)

Al.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets an aluminium contaminant maximum level for any fruit, vegetable or produce form in any jurisdiction. The register's aluminium limits are drinking-water and bottled-water parameters, infant-formula maximum levels, a food-contact plastics specific migration limit, toy migration limits, and permitted-additive levels for baked and starch foods; none of them regulates aluminium as a contaminant of produce. Aluminium is also the third most abundant element in the earth's crust and appears in produce largely as soil-derived and root-associated mineral content rather than as process contamination, so no near-neighbour read-across is supportable either. Under the government-limit-only method HMTc publishes no standalone aluminium number for this row.
Al.reference_method: Total aluminium by ICP-MS on every lot, reported to the applicant. Document any aluminium-containing processing aid, packaging contact or anti-caking agent, comply with the additive rules of every market of sale, and investigate any result that is an outlier against the applicant's own lot history.

Cr.screen_note: Total chromium is recorded as a SCREEN, not a protective ceiling. Dietary chromium is dominated by nutritionally essential Cr(III); the health-relevant species is Cr(VI), which is controlled separately by reflex speciation. A lot may satisfy this screen and still fail on Cr(VI), and the screen is excluded from the firm-limit count.
Cr.basis: food as listed in Cap 132V Part 2 Schedule; source unit mg/kg
Cr.label: Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 7 sets total chromium for vegetables other than pulses at 500 ug/kg, the only dietary total-chromium maximum level any credible government writes for this product form.
Cr.substantiation: Named as the sovereign total-chromium value for the vegetable class in its as-sold basis. Pulses are expressly outside this row (1000 ug/kg under the same item) and route to Category 27. Total chromium never satisfies the Cr(VI) cell.

Cr-VI.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum level for any solid food in any jurisdiction. The register's only INGESTED Cr(VI) parameters are drinking-water maxima (Australia NHMRC 2025, 50 ug/L, nhmrc2025_crvi_drinking_water_50; California SWRCB, 10 ug/L, us_ca_swrcb_2024_cr-vi_chromium-hexavalent_mcl_10ugl and ca_swrcb_crvi_drinking_water_10), which are water-basis parameters expressed per litre of a consumed liquid and supply no applicable ceiling for a solid produce row in this row's native basis; every remaining Cr(VI) row in the register is an article or material limit (toys, textiles, leather, fertilisers, electrical equipment). Chromium in produce is dominated by nutritionally essential Cr(III), and Cr(VI) is not stable in the plant matrix: fruit and vegetable tissue is an aqueous, organic-acid and ascorbate-rich reducing medium in which Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III), so a reported Cr(VI) value in this matrix reflects extraction conditions rather than the chromium species the consumer ingests. Hexavalent chromium is therefore bounded by the published total-chromium screen for this row (Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 7, 500 ug/kg) and controlled by reflex speciation rather than by a published number.
Cr-VI.reference_method: Total chromium by ICP-MS on every lot. Any total-chromium result at or above 100 ug/kg triggers Cr(VI) speciation by EN 15192 or EPA 6800 IC-ICP-MS isotope dilution; any quantifiable Cr(VI) at LOQ fails the lot. Cr(VI) is never published as a panel number.
Cr-VI.regulatory_basis: No jurisdiction sets a Cr(VI) maximum level for any solid food. The register's ingested Cr(VI) parameters are drinking-water maxima only (AU NHMRC 50 ug/L; California SWRCB 10 ug/L), which are water-basis and do not reach produce; every other Cr(VI) row is an article or material limit (EU 2009/48 toys, EU 2018/1513 textiles, EU 301/2014 leather, EU 2019/1009 fertilisers, EU RoHS). Neither drinking-water issuer is admitted to this category's credible set as a food regulator for a solid produce row. The total-chromium parent for this row is published.
Cr-VI.jurisdictions_checked: EU Reg. 2023/915; EU Reg. 2024/1987 (nickel); Switzerland VHK 817.022.15 (2026 metal/metalloid annex); Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2 Schedule; AU-NZ Food Standards Code Schedule 19; MERCOSUR GMC Res. 12/2011 and Paraguay Decreto 1335/2019; Israel MOH FCS-2016; Codex CXS 193-1995; US FDA (21 CFR, action levels)
